newsitem.title: USA: Virginia death row inmate gets clemency hearing.
newsitem.headline: Virginia death row inmate gets clemency hearing.

text.p: Virginia Gov. George Allen on Thursday held a clemency hearing for death row inmate Joseph O'Dell, who is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to review new DNA evidence he says proves his innocence.
O'Dell, 55, was convicted in 1985 of murdering 44-year-old secretary Helen Schartner and sentenced to death. He was scheduled to die by lethal injection on Dec. 18.
"The governor's advisers and attorneys did receive the clemency petition today and did meet with O'Dell's attorneys," a spokesman for Allen said.
Michelle Brace, a lawyer for the Virginia Capital Representation Resource Centre, said a petition for a stay of execution had also been filed with the Supreme Court.
"The governor won't make a decision until after the court has concluded all proceedings on the case," Brace said.
The Supreme Court tends to avoid hearing death penalty appeals, and Allen has granted clemency only once.
Death penalty opponents worldwide have rallied around O'Dell's case, pleading for review of the new DNA evidence, which they say shows that blood found on his shirt does not match that of the victim.
"That doesn't prove he's innocent but discredits what was presented at trial," said Richard Dieter, director of the Death Penalty Information Centre in Washington.
Death penalty opponents say a court of appeals refused to admit the DNA evidence and review the case because a submission deadline had expired.

Dieter added that O'Dell had represented himself at his trial and did not raise the proper objections that would have allowed him to preserve certain issues for appeal. If no objection is made to an issue during trial, the issue cannot be appealed.

Earlier on Thursday, dozens of demonstrators from human rights group Amnesty International, anti-death-penalty organisation Hands Off Cain and the Italian political party La Rete protested outside the U.S. Embassy in Rome.
Italy has no death penalty in civilian criminal cases and is among the most vociferous supporters of calls for the worldwide abolition of capital punishment.
Luciano Neri, a La Rete member and senator, said O'Dell's fate would be debated in Italy's upper house on Monday.
O'Dell's fate has also stirred the Vatican. Its semi-official newspaper L'Osservatore Romano has criticised what it called a legalistic approach to the case and urged a review.
